name: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation

clinicalPearls: Advanced heart failure is a distinct syndrome marked by refractoriness to conventional therapy, intolerance of guideline-dose neurohormonal antagonists, worsening renal function, poor cardiopulmonary reserve, and a low-output state with elevated pulmonary pressures; therapeutic goals shift toward surgical support of the failing heart (Harrison 22e p.2028).

Transplant candidacy generally requires refractory heart failure with a peak VO2 below ~14 mL/kg per min (below 12 if on beta blockers) or percent-predicted VO2 under 50%, combined with intolerance of disease-modifying therapy, cardiorenal syndrome, inotrope dependence, or need for an LVAS (Harrison 22e p.2028).

Age is not an absolute contraindication, but frailty is a relative one; BMI above 35 should prompt weight loss, eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 is a relative contraindication possibly requiring combined kidney transplant, and tobacco use in any form must cease for at least 6 months (Harrison 22e p.2028).

The transplanted heart is surgically denervated and unresponsive to sympathetic or parasympathetic stimuli; early postoperatively high-dose catecholamines are needed, and allograft bradycardia does NOT respond to atropine, so isoproterenol or temporary pacing is used (Harrison 22e p.2029).

Donor ischemia (out-of-body) time is typically limited to about 4 hours unless novel ex situ normothermic perfusion transport techniques are used; allocation considers urgency, waiting-list time, distance, and ABO blood group, while HLA matching is usually impractical given time constraints (Harrison 22e p.2029).

Acute cellular rejection (ACR) is a T cell-mediated process with myocardial lymphocytic infiltrates that occurs early and declines after about 6 months, whereas antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) is a noncellular, donor-specific antibody-driven process with complement fixation, endothelial swelling, and arteriolar vasculitis that carries worse allograft survival and predisposes to vasculopathy (Harrison 22e p.2029-2030).

Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is an accelerated, diffuse coronary intimal proliferation that is commonly clinically silent; intravascular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography is more sensitive than routine angiography for detection (Harrison 22e p.2030).
Angiographic CAV is present in roughly 30% of patients by 5 years and about 50% by 10 years after transplant; retransplantation is the only definitive therapy for advanced CAV (Harrison 22e p.2030).

Continuous-flow LVAS generate forward flow dependent on the pressure gradient between the LV cavity and aorta, so flow is critically sensitive to systemic blood pressure; because pulse is often undetectable, blood pressure is measured by Doppler (mean/opening pressure) and the target mean arterial pressure is at or below 90 mmHg (Harrison 22e p.2032).

LVAS-related shear stress can cause low-grade hemolysis and acquired von Willebrand disease (loss of high-molecular-weight vWF multimers), predisposing to gastrointestinal bleeding from intestinal arteriovenous malformations and to iron-deficiency anemia (Harrison 22e p.2032).
Lactate dehydrogenase is an excellent though nonspecific biomarker of hemolysis and can herald pump thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.2032).

Posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders are usually Epstein-Barr virus driven and are the most frequent malignancy; solid cancers most often manifest as basal- and squamous-cell skin malignancies, so routine sunscreen is advised (Harrison 22e p.2030).
harrison.pathophysiology: In advanced (stage D) heart failure the myocardium can no longer maintain adequate output despite maximal medical therapy, producing a low cardiac output state with elevated filling and pulmonary pressures, intolerance of neurohormonal antagonists, and progressive cardiorenal dysfunction. Cardiac transplantation replaces the failing heart with an allograft that is surgically denervated, so it depends initially on circulating catecholamines and cannot mount reflex heart-rate responses. Allograft rejection follows two mechanisms: ACR, a T cell-mediated lymphocytic assault on donor myocardium (perivenular in mild disease, diffuse interstitial with myocyte necrosis and hemorrhage in severe disease), and AMR, an antibody/complement-mediated injury with immunoglobulin deposition, endothelial swelling, interstitial edema, and arteriolar vasculitis. Over the long term, immunologic insults (brain death, ischemia-reperfusion, alloimmunity) combined with nonimmunologic metabolic factors (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, dysglycemia from chronic immunosuppression) drive cardiac allograft vasculopathy, a diffuse fibrotic intimal proliferation narrowing the coronary tree. For mechanical support, continuous-flow LVAS divert blood from the LV apex to the aorta via a pump whose output depends on the LV-to-aorta pressure gradient; the non-physiologic flow path imposes shear stress that degrades von Willebrand factor multimers and causes hemolysis. LV unloading lowers right-sided afterload, but increased device flow raises RV preload and the displaced septum reduces RV contractile efficiency, promoting RV dilatation and maladaptation.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of advanced/refractory heart failure warranting evaluation: restrictive and infiltrative cardiomyopathy (e.g., amyloidosis), congenital heart disease, and chronic-infection-associated cardiomyopathy (Chagas disease, viral hepatitis-related, tuberculosis)
Allograft dysfunction differential after transplant: acute cellular rejection vs antibody-mediated rejection vs cardiac allograft vasculopathy vs primary graft dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Surveillance endomyocardial biopsy to grade and monitor rejection
Immunofluorescence for immunoglobulin deposition and complement fixation, plus circulating donor-specific antibody testing, when AMR is suspected
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing for peak VO2 to assess transplant/LVAS candidacy

Invasive hemodynamic assessment of pulmonary vascular resistance and transpulmonary gradient (PVR >3 Wood units or transpulmonary gradient >15 are relative transplant contraindications unless reactive)
Intravascular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography (more sensitive than angiography) and noninvasive coronary flow reserve for CAV detection and prognosis
Prospective or virtual cross-match in allosensitized recipients with preformed antibodies
Doppler-derived mean arterial pressure measurement in continuous-flow LVAS patients
Lactate dehydrogenase as a hemolysis biomarker to screen for pump thrombosis
redFlags: Hemodynamic compromise during acute cellular rejection signals severe rejection and warrants rescue polyclonal antibody therapy with corticosteroids
Suspected LVAD thrombosis carries a high mortality if pump exchange or transplant is not performed; rising LDH may herald it
Neurologic events (ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke) are major hemocompatibility-related complications of LVAS
Driveline infection (occurs in 20-50% of LVAS patients by 5 years) predisposes to thrombosis and neurologic complications
Gastrointestinal bleeding from acquired von Willebrand disease and intestinal arteriovenous malformations
Progressive right ventricular failure and congestion after LVAS implantation
harrison.prognosis: More than 150,000 patients have undergone cardiac transplantation worldwide, with 1-year survival above 80%, median survival of ~12.5 years, and conditional survival of ~14.8 years for those surviving the first year. With the fully magnetically levitated HeartMate 3 LVAS, median survival exceeds 5 years (about 60% survival at 5 years), and in younger patients (under 50) without comorbidity and an uncomplicated course the 5-year survival can rival transplantation (~75%). Without such support, patients with severe refractory systolic heart failure (peak VO2 <12 mL/kg per min or inotrope dependence) often have a median survival under 1 year. CAV grade correlates with prognosis and remains a leading limit on late allograft survival.
pitfalls: Treating allograft bradycardia with atropine, which is ineffective because the transplanted heart is denervated (use isoproterenol or pacing instead)
Relying on routine coronary angiography alone, which underdiagnoses early cardiac allograft vasculopathy compared with intravascular ultrasound or OCT
Attempting to palpate or auscultate a peripheral pulse for blood pressure in continuous-flow LVAS patients, who often have no detectable pulse; Doppler must be used
Overlooking acquired von Willebrand disease as the cause of GI bleeding in LVAS patients
Continuing aspirin in HeartMate 3 patients, which increases nonsurgical bleeding; its elimination (with a vitamin K antagonist targeting INR 2-3) reduces bleeding-related hospitalizations
Failing to anticipate right ventricular failure after LV unloading by an LVAS
harrison.severityClassification: Cardiac allograft vasculopathy is graded by the ISHLT 2010 scheme as CAV0 (absent), CAV1 (mild), CAV2 (moderate), and CAV3 (severe), based on extent of angiographic disease and presence of allograft dysfunction by echocardiography or restrictive physiology. Transplant allocation urgency is tiered, with the highest status for critically ill patients on ECMO or temporary biventricular mechanical support, then those needing daily invasive hemodynamic monitoring plus IV inotropes or with durable LVAD complications, and lower status for ambulatory patients stable at home.
